topics.name: Introduction
topics.description: Inference engineering is the practice of making generative AI models faster, less expensive, and more reliable to serve in production. It spans the full stack from CUDA kernels and GPU architecture to Kubernetes autoscaling and multi-cloud capacity management. The field emerged alongside the explosion of open models and the shift from pay-per-token APIs to dedicated deployments, where engineers own latency, throughput, cost, and uptime directly.

subtopics.name: Open vs Closed Models
subtopics.description: Closed models are accessed exclusively through a vendor API; the weights are never released. Open models publish their weights for download and self-hosting. For inference engineers, this distinction determines the entire problem space: closed models require no infrastructure but offer no control over latency, cost, or configuration, while open models require building and operating a full inference stack but give complete control over every layer of it.

subtopics.name: Inference vs. Training
subtopics.description: Training is the process of learning model weights from data. Inference is serving those weights in production to generate outputs. Training runs are compute-intensive batch jobs; inference is a continuous, latency-sensitive service. Where training success is measured in loss curves, inference success is measured in time to first token, tokens per second, and uptime.

subtopics.name: Time to First Token
subtopics.description: TTFT measures how long it takes for a user to receive the first output token after submitting a request. It is determined primarily by the prefill phase and by queue time. For streaming applications like chatbots, TTFT is the most visible latency signal and directly affects perceived responsiveness.

subtopics.name: Tokens Per Second
subtopics.description: TPS measures how many tokens are delivered to the user per second after the first token. It is determined by the decode phase and reflects memory bandwidth efficiency. Per-user TPS (also called perceived TPS) is a latency metric; total TPS across the inference service is a throughput metric.

subtopics.name: Inter-Token Latency
subtopics.description: ITL is the time between successive generated tokens during decode. An ITL of 10 milliseconds corresponds to 100 tokens per second. It is the per-step measure underlying TPS and is directly tied to how quickly the GPU can complete a single decode forward pass.

subtopics.name: Latency vs. Throughput
subtopics.description: Lower latency means faster responses per user; higher throughput means more total requests served per unit time. These goals are often in tension. Increasing batch size improves throughput but worsens per-user latency. Choosing the right balance is one of the primary decisions in configuring an inference service.

subtopics.name: Latency Percentiles
subtopics.description: Mean latency hides outliers. LLM response times follow a right-skewed distribution, so engineers measure P50, P90, P95, and P99. A P99 of several seconds means one in a hundred users has a poor experience even if the median is fast. Reducing P90/P99 latency is as important as reducing average latency.

subtopics.name: End-to-End Metrics
subtopics.description: End-to-end latency includes inference time, network round-trip, queue time, and client-side overhead. Inference-only metrics tell you how well the model server performs; end-to-end metrics tell you what users actually experience. When inference time is fast but end-to-end time is slow, the bottleneck is in infrastructure or client code, not the GPU.

subtopics.name: Real-Time Factor
subtopics.description: RTF measures how quickly an ASR system can process audio relative to its duration. A system that transcribes one hour of audio in six seconds has an RTF of 600x. It is the standard throughput metric for long-file transcription workloads and improves roughly linearly with the number of GPUs used for parallel chunk processing.

subtopics.name: Shared vs. Dedicated Inf.
subtopics.description: Shared inference means sending requests to a public API and paying per token. Dedicated inference means renting GPUs and running your own model server, paying per GPU-hour. Shared inference is simpler and has no cold start, but dedicated inference offers control over latency, cost at scale, model customization, and uptime. Most products start shared and move to dedicated as traffic grows.

subtopics.name: The Inference Stack
subtopics.description: A complete inference system has three layers: runtime, infrastructure, and tooling. The runtime layer optimizes a single model on a single instance using techniques like batching, caching, quantization, and speculation. The infrastructure layer scales across clusters, regions, and cloud providers while maintaining uptime. The tooling layer provides the right level of abstraction for engineers to control the system productively. All three must work together for mission-critical inference at scale.

subtopics.name: Prefill & Decode Phases
subtopics.description: LLM inference has two distinct phases. Prefill processes the entire input sequence in parallel to build the KV cache and is compute-bound. Decode generates output tokens one at a time by reading model weights from memory and is memory-bound. Each phase has different bottlenecks and responds to different optimization techniques.

subtopics.name: Online vs. Offline Inf.
subtopics.description: Online inference serves real-time user-facing requests where latency matters. Offline inference processes large batches of data asynchronously where throughput and cost matter more than per-request speed. The same model, like Whisper for transcription, may need separate deployments for each use case because the optimal configurations differ significantly.

subtopics.name: Asynchronous Inference
subtopics.description: Asynchronous inference is a fire-and-forget request model where the client submits a job, receives an immediate acknowledgment, and retrieves the result later via a webhook. It is suited for throughput-sensitive, latency-insensitive workloads like bulk document embedding or corpus transcription. Async jobs have much longer time limits than synchronous requests and require robust server-side queuing.

subtopics.name: AI-Native Applications
subtopics.description: AI-native applications are products where generative models power the core user experience, from code editors and voice agents to customer support and media generation. Each category has different inference requirements. Agents generate many inference calls per user action; chat applications prioritize TTFT; voice applications need low end-to-end latency for natural conversation.

subtopics.name: Consumer vs. B2B
subtopics.description: Consumer applications are cost-sensitive and have unpredictable traffic spikes, requiring flexible autoscaling and low marginal cost. Business-to-business applications prioritize uptime and consistent low latency, as they often sit in the critical path of revenue-generating workflows. Compliance requirements, including data residency and regulatory certifications, are more common in enterprise deployments.

subtopics.name: Reasoning Models
subtopics.description: Reasoning models generate an intermediate thinking sequence before producing their final output, adding a third token sequence alongside the input and output. This reasoning trace increases total token count significantly and changes inference economics: TTFT is higher, total latency is longer, and output token costs dominate. Inference engineers must account for the variable and sometimes very long reasoning sequences when sizing infrastructure and setting latency budgets.

subtopics.name: Model Selection
subtopics.description: The most important decision in model performance optimization is which model to use. Smaller models with fewer parameters are faster and cheaper to serve than larger ones. The goal is to find the smallest model that meets quality requirements for the task. Model architecture also determines which inference engines and optimization techniques are available, so popular architectures with broad tooling support are preferable.

subtopics.name: Model Evaluation
subtopics.description: Model evaluation, or evals, is the practice of systematically measuring model quality for a specific task or domain. Standard intelligence benchmarks like MMLU measure general capabilities but can be gamed; product-specific evals that test real use cases provide more reliable signal. High-confidence evals are a prerequisite before investing in inference optimization, ensuring the model is actually useful before making it fast.

subtopics.name: Fine-Tuning
subtopics.description: Fine-tuning takes a pretrained foundation model and adapts it to a specific domain by training on additional labeled data. A small fine-tuned model can match a much larger general model on constrained tasks like text-to-SQL. Smaller models are faster and cheaper to serve, so fine-tuning is one of the highest-leverage tools for hitting latency and cost targets.

subtopics.name: Distillation
subtopics.description: Distillation trains a smaller student model to emulate a larger teacher model by exposing it to the teacher's probability distributions, not just its final outputs. Unlike fine-tuning on synthetic data, distillation transfers the teacher's reasoning behavior. The resulting student model is smaller and faster while retaining much of the teacher's quality on the same tasks.

subtopics.name: Compute
subtopics.description: A GPU's compute capability is determined by its Streaming Multiprocessors (SMs), each containing CUDA Cores for general arithmetic and Tensor Cores for matrix multiply-accumulate operations. Tensor Cores are the primary resource for inference, executing the matmuls that make up the majority of forward pass computation. GPU compute is measured in peak Tensor Core FLOPS at a given precision, and roughly doubles with each new NVIDIA architecture generation.

topics.name: Neural Networks
topics.description: A neural network is a layered structure of nodes where each node applies a learned weight matrix and bias to its input. Multiple layers connected in sequence form the foundation for all generative AI models. Inference engineers need a working model of how neural networks compute outputs to understand where performance bottlenecks arise.

subtopics.name: Encoder-Decoder Arch.
subtopics.description: Neural networks can be organized as encoder-only, decoder-only, or encoder-decoder models. Modern LLMs are decoder-only. Encoder-only models like BERT are used for text embeddings and classification. Encoder-decoder models like Whisper use an encoder to process input into an internal representation and a decoder to generate output tokens autoregressively. Each architecture has different inference characteristics and tooling requirements.

topics.name: Large Language Models
topics.description: An LLM is a decoder-only transformer with three main components: an embedding layer that converts input tokens to vectors, a stack of transformer blocks that process those vectors, and an output language modeling head that converts the final hidden states into a probability distribution over the vocabulary. The configuration file for an open model specifies all architectural details including layer count, hidden dimensions, and attention heads.

subtopics.name: Transformer Blocks
subtopics.description: Transformer blocks are the repeated hidden layers of an LLM. Each block contains an attention sublayer, a feed-forward neural network sublayer, and normalization layers. The feed-forward network holds the majority of model parameters, while attention is the most computationally complex operation per token.

subtopics.name: Attention Mechanism
subtopics.description: Attention is the mechanism transformers use to relate each token to all previous tokens via query, key, and value projections. During decode, each new token attends to every prior token, and the KV cache stores precomputed keys and values to avoid recomputation. Attention is the most expensive and most heavily optimized operation in LLM inference.

subtopics.name: KV Cache
subtopics.description: The KV cache stores the key and value tensors computed during attention for each previously processed token. Without it, attention would require recomputing every prior token on each decode step, making inference prohibitively slow. The KV cache lives in GPU memory and its size grows with sequence length and batch size, making it a major target for memory management techniques.

subtopics.name: Mixture of Experts (MoE)
subtopics.description: Mixture of Experts models replace dense linear layers with a set of smaller expert matrices, activating only a subset of experts per token via a learned router. A model like Qwen3-235B activates only 22 billion of its 235 billion parameters per forward pass, making single-user inference efficient. In batched production serving, different tokens activate different experts, so nearly all parameters are active across the batch.

topics.name: Image & Video Models
topics.description: Image and video models are specialized artificial intelligence architectures designed to process, interpret, and generate visual data. These models utilize techniques like convolutional neural networks (CNNs), transformers, and diffusion processes to analyze pixel patterns for tasks such as object detection, image classification, and video frame synthesis.

subtopics.name: Diffusion Models
subtopics.description: Diffusion models generate images by starting from random noise and iteratively denoising it over 30 to 50 steps, guided by a text prompt. Each step runs the denoiser twice, once with conditioning and once without, to apply classifier-free guidance. The entire process operates in a low-dimensional latent space rather than full pixel space to make attention computationally feasible.

subtopics.name: Image Generation Arch.
subtopics.description: Image generation models are pipelines of multiple components: a text encoder that converts the prompt into conditioning, a denoising model that iteratively refines a latent representation from noise into an image, and a variational autoencoder that converts the final latent to pixels. The denoising model is the largest and most compute-intensive component and runs up to 100 forward passes per image generation.

subtopics.name: Few-Step Image Generation
subtopics.description: Few-step image generation models produce usable images in eight or fewer denoising steps by training the model to collapse the standard 30 to 50 step process into a fraction of the iterations. Techniques include latent consistency distillation and adversarial training, both of which teach the model to reach high-quality outputs in fewer passes. They are a strong fit for latency-sensitive use cases like real-time filters, but produce noticeably lower quality than full-step models and are a model selection decision rather than an inference optimization technique.

subtopics.name: Video Generation Models
subtopics.description: Video generation models extend image generation to three-dimensional latent space, representing width, height, and time simultaneously. They run the same number of denoising steps as image models but process far more data per step. Attention over the full video latent space dominates compute time, making video generation the most resource-intensive common inference workload.

topics.name: Bottleneck Analysis
topics.description: Bottleneck analysis identifies whether a given inference workload is limited by compute or by memory bandwidth, which determines which optimizations will actually improve performance. The core tool is the ops:byte ratio: comparing a GPU's peak FLOPS against its peak memory bandwidth reveals the hardware's balance point, and comparing a model operation's arithmetic intensity against that balance point reveals whether it is compute-bound or memory-bound. LLM prefill and image generation are compute-bound; LLM decode is memory-bound.

subtopics.name: Ops:Byte Ratio
subtopics.description: The ops:byte ratio is a property of GPU hardware that expresses the balance between compute throughput and memory bandwidth. It is calculated by dividing peak FLOPS by peak memory bandwidth, and sets the threshold that separates compute-bound from memory-bound workloads on that device. Different GPU generations have very different ops:byte ratios, which is why an optimization that works well on one generation may have no effect on another.

subtopics.name: Arithmetic Intensity
subtopics.description: Arithmetic intensity is a property of an algorithm: the number of floating-point operations performed per byte of memory read or written. A large matrix multiplication has high arithmetic intensity because the same weights participate in many operations per load; a decode forward pass has low arithmetic intensity because each weight is loaded from VRAM and used once per token. Comparing a workload's arithmetic intensity against the GPU's ops:byte ratio is the fastest way to diagnose whether adding compute or adding bandwidth would help.

subtopics.name: Roofline Model
subtopics.description: The roofline model is a visual framework for reasoning about hardware performance limits. It plots arithmetic intensity on the x-axis against achievable performance on the y-axis, with two ceilings: a diagonal memory bandwidth ceiling for low-intensity workloads and a horizontal compute ceiling for high-intensity ones. A workload's position relative to these ceilings shows not just whether it is compute-bound or memory-bound, but how far it sits from the hardware's theoretical maximum — which tells you how much headroom remains before an optimization hits a hard limit.

subtopics.name: LLM Bottlenecks
subtopics.description: LLM prefill is compute-bound because it processes the entire input sequence as one large matrix multiplication, performing many operations per byte loaded. LLM decode is memory-bound because it generates tokens one at a time via vector-matrix multiplications that require loading all model weights from memory for each token while performing relatively few arithmetic operations.

topics.name: Attention Optimization
topics.description: Attention optimization refers to techniques designed to improve the computational efficiency and memory usage of the attention mechanism within transformer models. Because standard attention scales quadratically with input sequence length, these optimizations aim to reduce computation and memory overhead. By streamlining how tokens interact with one another, these methods allow models to process longer inputs faster and run on hardware with less available memory.

subtopics.name: Image & Video Bottlenecks
subtopics.description: Image and video generation models are compute-bound because each denoising step applies attention over the entire latent space in parallel, similar to LLM prefill. The models are also relatively small, so memory bandwidth is not the limiting factor. Optimizations focus on FLOPS efficiency rather than memory traffic reduction.

subtopics.name: FlashAttention
subtopics.description: FlashAttention is a series of hand-optimized CUDA kernels that compute attention with fewer reads and writes to GPU memory by fusing the attention algorithm into a single kernel. Standard attention stores intermediate matrices to memory between steps; FlashAttention eliminates those round-trips. FlashAttention 3 targets Hopper GPUs and FlashAttention 4 targets Blackwell GPUs.

subtopics.name: PagedAttention
subtopics.description: PagedAttention stores the KV cache in fixed-size pages rather than a single contiguous memory block, allowing it to be distributed across GPU memory without fragmentation. It uses a lookup table to access pages on demand, reducing memory waste from over-allocation and enabling more requests to share GPU memory. It is the memory management technique that made vLLM's high throughput possible.

subtopics.name: Attention Variants
subtopics.description: Newer attention algorithms reduce the quadratic time complexity of standard attention. Sliding window attention limits each token to attending to the nearest w tokens, turning O(N²) into O(Nw). Linear attention approximates the softmax with a linear-time kernel. Compressed attention periodically compresses earlier context. These variants trade off some quality for better scaling on long sequences.

subtopics.name: Memory
subtopics.description: GPU memory determines what fits on a single device and how fast data can move through the compute units. VRAM capacity sets the upper limit on model size and KV cache; VRAM bandwidth determines how quickly the decode phase can load weights per token. Modern datacenter GPUs use high-bandwidth memory (HBM) in generations HBM3, HBM3e, and HBM4, stacked directly on the GPU die to maximize bandwidth.

H100 and H200 GPUs remain among the most widely deployed inference accelerators due to their maturity, broad software support, and relative availability compared to newer generations.

subtopics.name: Blackwell
subtopics.description: The Blackwell architecture, released in late 2024 with the B200 and B300, added FP4 Tensor Cores and new microscaling number formats including MXFP8, MXFP4, and NVFP4. B200 GPUs offer approximately 5 petaFLOPS of FP8 compute and up to 8 TB/s of memory bandwidth. They are the current gold standard for demanding inference workloads including large LLMs and video generation.

subtopics.name: Instances & Interconnects
subtopics.description: Within a node, NVLink connects GPUs one-to-one at up to 1800 GB/s on Blackwell, and NVSwitch creates an all-to-all fabric across all eight GPUs. Between nodes, InfiniBand provides inter-node connectivity at substantially lower bandwidth than NVLink. Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) partitions a single GPU into up to seven isolated slices, each with dedicated compute and memory, allowing small models to run on fractions of a high-end GPU without resource contention.

subtopics.name: Sizing & Procurement
subtopics.description: Estimating GPU requirements starts with VRAM: roughly 1 GB per billion parameters at FP8 for weights, plus at least 50 percent headroom for the KV cache. This total is rounded up to the nearest available instance size. Cloud GPUs are available from hyperscalers like AWS and GCP, neoclouds like CoreWeave and Nebius, and spot markets; large deployments combine reserved instances for baseline load with on-demand and spot capacity for bursts.

Every inference engine, framework, and library in the NVIDIA ecosystem depends on CUDA, including cuBLAS — NVIDIA's optimized implementation of standard linear algebra routines and the default backend for matrix multiplications in most inference pipelines. Kernel selection is choosing the best existing kernel for a specific operation; kernel fusion combines sequential kernels into one to eliminate unnecessary reads and writes to VRAM between operations. Libraries like cuBLAS, CUTLASS, CuTe, and FlashInfer provide pre-built kernels for common inference operations, and most inference engines perform kernel selection automatically.

topics.name: Quantization
topics.description: Quantization converts model weights and other values from their native precision to a lower-precision format. Cutting precision in half doubles memory bandwidth for decode and enables twice the FLOPS for prefill on compatible Tensor Cores. The tradeoff is potential quality loss from reduced numerical precision, which can compound across the many calculations in a forward pass.

subtopics.name: Quantization-Aware Training
subtopics.description: Quantization-aware training computes scale factors and optimizes model weights jointly during training so the final model is already calibrated for the target low-precision format. This produces better quality at low precision than post-training quantization but requires retraining the model from scratch or from a checkpoint. Some labs release models trained this way, such as GPT-OSS in MXFP4.

subtopics.description: Post-training quantization converts finished model weights to lower precision after training is complete, using a small calibration dataset to compute per-layer scale factors that minimize the gap between quantized and original outputs. It is the standard approach for most deployments since it requires no retraining and can be applied to any existing model. The leading tool is NVIDIA ModelOpt, which exports quantized models in formats compatible with all major inference engines.

It integrates with PyTorch and exports quantized models directly to TensorRT-LLM, vLLM, and SGLang. topics.name: Speculative Decoding
topics.description: Speculative decoding takes advantage of spare compute during memory-bound decode by generating multiple draft tokens and validating them in a single forward pass. If the target model accepts N draft tokens, the forward pass produces N+1 tokens instead of one. The performance gain depends on draft token cost, draft sequence length, and acceptance rate, which decreases at higher temperatures and larger batch sizes.

subtopics.name: N-gram
subtopics.description: N-gram speculation builds a dictionary during prefill that maps token prefixes to observed n-gram continuations from the input. During decode, generated tokens are looked up in this dictionary and matching suffixes become draft tokens with no separate model required. It is most effective for code completion, where output frequently mirrors input syntax, and can produce very long draft sequences with high acceptance rates in that domain.

subtopics.name: Draft-Target Decoding
subtopics.description: Draft-target speculation uses a small draft model, typically at least ten times smaller than the target, to generate draft tokens for the target model to verify. The draft model should share the same tokenizer and general behavior as the target, often being a smaller member of the same model family. It is the simplest speculation method to set up but introduces the most overhead due to running a separate model.

subtopics.name: EAGLE
subtopics.description: EAGLE is a purpose-built speculation method where a small draft model is trained to accept hidden states from the target model as input. By seeing the target's internal representations, EAGLE achieves higher acceptance rates and longer draft sequences (up to eight tokens) than using a general-purpose small model. It integrates into the same forward pass as the target model, eliminating the orchestration overhead of separate draft and target model runs.

topics.name: Caching
topics.description: Caching reuses previously computed KV values to avoid redundant prefill computation across requests that share common context. It is one of the most impactful techniques for reducing TTFT in workloads with long system prompts or multi-turn conversations. This group covers the approaches, storage tiers, routing implications, and long-context strategies that make caching effective at scale.

A related concern is cache-aware routing, which directs requests to replicas most likely to already hold the relevant cached prefix.

Moving less frequently accessed KV blocks to slower storage frees VRAM for active requests. subtopics.description: In deployments with multiple replicas, cache-aware routing directs requests to the replica most likely to have a matching prefix already in its KV cache. Without this, a user in a long conversation may hit different replicas each turn, getting cache misses that increase latency. A global KV cache stored on networked SSD allows all replicas to eventually access any cached sequence.

subtopics.description: Long sequences produce KV caches large enough to strain GPU memory, slow down decode, and increase prefill time. topics.name: Model Parallelism
topics.description: When a model is too large to fit on a single GPU, or when serving latency requires more compute than one device can provide, model parallelism distributes the workload across multiple GPUs or nodes. This group covers the three parallelism strategies and their trade-offs in terms of communication overhead, latency, and hardware requirements.

subtopics.name: Pipeline Parallelism
subtopics.description: Pipeline Parallelism splits an LLM's layers into sequential stages and assigns each stage to a different GPU or node. Unlike Tensor Parallelism, each GPU holds complete layers rather than layer fragments. It introduces pipeline bubbles where GPUs wait for preceding stages, reducing efficiency. It is used for multi-node inference with dense models, typically combined with Tensor Parallelism within each node.

subtopics.name: Tensor Parallelism
subtopics.description: Tensor Parallelism splits each layer's weight matrices across multiple GPUs and distributes the matmul computation. Each GPU handles a shard of each layer and the results are combined via an all-reduce operation before the next layer. It reduces per-user latency by sharing both VRAM and compute across GPUs, but requires fast NVLink interconnects and is not well-suited for multi-node deployments.

subtopics.name: Expert Parallelism
subtopics.description: Expert Parallelism distributes MoE experts across GPUs so each GPU hosts multiple complete experts. Tokens are routed to the GPU holding their activated experts, and each expert runs independently within a single GPU without splitting across multiple. EP has lower inter-GPU communication overhead than Tensor Parallelism and scales well to multi-node deployments via InfiniBand.

subtopics.name: Multi-Node Inference
subtopics.description: Multi-node inference spreads a model across more than eight GPUs using InfiniBand for inter-node communication. It is necessary for the largest models where a single node lacks sufficient VRAM for weights and KV cache. InfiniBand bandwidth is an order of magnitude lower than NVLink, so parallelism strategies must minimize cross-node communication. For MoE models, Expert Parallelism is preferred over Tensor Parallelism between nodes.

topics.name: Disaggregation
topics.description: Disaggregation separates the prefill and decode phases onto independent GPU instances that can scale separately. The prefill engine processes the input sequence and sends the resulting KV cache to the decode engine via the hardware interconnect. This removes the resource contention between compute-heavy prefill and memory-heavy decode. Disaggregation is most effective at high traffic volumes, for large models, and with prefill-heavy workloads like code editors.

The ratio of prefill to decode engines is configurable at runtime and can shift as traffic patterns change. This dynamic allocation prevents the prefill queue from becoming a bottleneck and avoids wasting decode engine resources on prefill-heavy traffic.

subtopics.name: Text-to-Speech (TTS)
subtopics.description: Modern TTS models like Orpheus TTS are fine-tuned LLMs with an expanded vocabulary that includes audio tokens. They generate audio token sequences decoded to waveforms by a small audio decoder. The key performance metrics are time to first byte of audio (TTFB) and the number of concurrent real-time streams a single GPU replica can sustain, rather than raw token throughput.

resources.title: What is text to speech?
Text-to-Speech
TTS Models
Create your own voices with Gemini 3.8 text-to-speech

subtopics.name: Streaming TTS
subtopics.description: Real-time TTS streams audio continuously over WebSockets rather than returning a complete file after generation finishes. The audio decoder converts token streams to waveforms as they are generated, implemented in compiled PyTorch with dynamic batching. After tuning the inference engine and decoder, the primary performance lever is how many concurrent real-time streams a single GPU replica can sustain.

resources.title: Streaming TTS
Streaming Text-to-Speech
Streaming Speech to Text Models - Kyutai vs Whisper

subtopics.name: Speech-to-Speech Models
subtopics.description: Speech-to-speech models unify ASR, reasoning, and TTS into a single model by expanding the LLM vocabulary with audio input and output tokens, eliminating the latency of cascading three separate models in sequence. Current closed models like OpenAI's gpt-4o-realtime exist but remain more expensive and less capable than well-tuned cascading pipelines of dedicated ASR, LLM, and TTS models. Open speech-to-speech models are an active research area without commercially viable options at the time of writing.

resources.title: What Is Speech-to-Speech? Uses, Benefits & How It Works
Speech-to-Speech LLMs

topics.name: Image & Video Generation
topics.description: Image and video generation inference is compute-bound rather than memory-bound, making it a different optimization problem from LLM serving. This group covers the production patterns, kernel choices, and parallelism techniques specific to diffusion model deployment.

resources.title: Understanding AI Image Generation: Models, Tools, and Techniques
Understanding AI Video Generation History: Key Concepts and Impact

subtopics.name: Image Generation Inference
subtopics.description: Production image generation inference uses SGLang Diffusion, TensorRT, or hand-optimized PyTorch. The most important optimization target is the attention kernel, where FlashAttention 3 or 4 outperforms the default on Hopper and Blackwell respectively. GEMM kernels for linear layers can be quantized to FP8 safely. Torch compilation with manual kernel plugins caches the compiled engine to avoid multi-minute recompilation on every cold start.

resources.title: Image Generation Inference Mechanics
What Is Inference in Generative AI: How It Differs From Traditional Model Inference
Diffusion Models for AI Image Generation
Why Does Diffusion Work Better than Auto-Regression?

subtopics.name: Video Generation Inference
subtopics.description: Video generation models run on full nodes of eight GPUs with a batch size of one because the latent space is too large to batch effectively. Attention over the three-dimensional video latent space consumes 70 to 80 percent of compute time and is the primary optimization target. Attention caching techniques that reuse outputs from previous timesteps or transformer layers can improve speed by 30 to 40 percent.

resources.title: Cache-DiT
TeaCache: Timestep Embedding Tells: It's Time to Cache for Video Diffusion Model
Video Generation Models

topics.name: Containerization
topics.description: Containerization packages an inference service and all its dependencies into a Docker image that runs consistently across environments. Inference containers include the CUDA toolkit, Python packages, the inference engine, and any system libraries like ffmpeg for audio processing. Using a pinned dependency tree prevents breaking changes from affecting running services and ensures reproducible builds.

resources.title: Docker Documentation
Kubernetes Documentation
What is containerization?
Containerization Explained

subtopics.name: Dependency Management
subtopics.description: Inference dependency chains are long and fragile due to the tight coupling between CUDA versions, framework versions, and hardware architectures. Pinning exact versions of every dependency prevents unexpected breakage when upstream packages release updates. Containers for newly released models often initially depend on pre-release software builds and need to be rebuilt on stable releases within days of the model launch.

resources.title: Kubernetes Documentation
Dependency Management
Production in Inference Engineering

subtopics.name: NIMs
subtopics.description: NIMs are pre-built Docker containers provided by NVIDIA for popular open models, available as flexible multi-LLM containers or as GPU- and model-specific optimized containers. They provide a ready-made starting point for serving common architectures without building a custom container from scratch. For maximum control and custom configurations, starting from a less opinionated base image and building up is generally preferable.

resources.title: NVIDIA NIM for Developers
NVIDIA NIM Microservices
NVIDIA NIM in Docker
How to Self-Host LLMs and Multi-Modal AI Models with NVIDIA NIM in 5 Minutes

topics.name: Autoscaling
topics.description: Autoscaling dynamically adjusts the number of active model replicas to match incoming traffic, maintaining latency SLAs while minimizing idle GPU spend. Kubernetes is the standard orchestration layer, scaling replicas within a cluster based on traffic signals and utilization metrics. Key configuration parameters are min replicas, max replicas, the autoscaling window, the scale-down delay, and the concurrency target per replica.

resources.title: Autoscaling endpoints for LLM inference
Autoscaling Inference Endpoints
Best practices for autoscaling large language model (LLM) inference workloads
Autoscaling your AI agent under load

subtopics.name: Continuous Batching
subtopics.description: Continuous batching operates at the token level, swapping requests in and out of the batch as they complete individual tokens rather than waiting for a full batch to finish. This keeps GPU utilization high and minimizes the latency penalty of batching compared to static or dynamic batching. All major inference engines implement continuous batching by default.

resources.title: Continuous batching
Continuous Batching: Optimizing LLM Inference Throughput
How to Scale LLM Applications With Continuous Batching!
Continuous Batching - How LLM Servers Keep the GPU Full

subtopics.name: Cold Starts
subtopics.description: A cold start is the time from zero replicas to serving the first request, including GPU provisioning, container image loading, model weight loading, and inference engine startup or compilation. Reducing cold start time is essential for autoscaling systems to scale down confidently and scale up responsively. Key techniques include quantized weights, local weight caching near the GPU instances, and caching compiled inference engines to disk.

resources.title: Autoscaling endpoints for LLM inference
Autoscaling for LLM Inference Serving and Cold Starts
GPU Cold Start on Serverless LLM Inference: 4 Fixes That Actually Work (2026)

subtopics.name: Routing & Load Balancing
subtopics.description: Routers make request-level decisions about which replica to send a request to, considering factors like KV cache prefix match and LoRA availability. Load balancers make system-level decisions to distribute traffic evenly across replicas. In systems with prefix caching, naive round-robin load balancing misses cache opportunities; intelligent routing increases cache hit rates and reduces TTFT.

resources.title: LLM Inference Serving: Architecture, Routing & Auto-Scaling
LLM Model Routing: Route Queries to the Right Model Automatically
LLM Load Balancing: Concepts, Strategies & Best Practices
Auto Routing Fully Explained

topics.name: Multi-Cloud
topics.description: Multi-cloud inference distributes GPU capacity across providers and regions to maximize availability, minimize latency, and meet data residency requirements. This group covers procurement strategy, capacity management, geographic routing, and the reliability patterns that make large-scale inference resilient to hardware and provider failures.

resources.title: Visit the Dedicated Cloud Computing Roadmap
How to Do Agentic AI Inference in a Multicloud, Multi-Model World
What is multicloud?
Multi-Cloud GPU Strategy: How to Avoid AI Infrastructure Vendor Lock-In

subtopics.name: GPU Procurement
subtopics.description: Cloud GPUs are available from hyperscalers like AWS and GCP, GPU-focused neoclouds like CoreWeave and Nebius, and secondary markets. Procurement mechanisms include reserved instances for predictable baseline load at discounted rates, on-demand instances for flexibility, and spot instances for cost-sensitive batch workloads that tolerate preemption. Large-scale deployments typically combine all three across multiple providers.

resources.title: Multi-Cloud GPU Strategy: How to Avoid AI Infrastructure Vendor Lock-In
Multi-Cloud GPU Strategy: Definition, Benefits, and Implementation

subtopics.name: LoRA-Aware Routing
subtopics.description: LoRA fine-tune weights are small adapter layers loaded on top of a base model to specialize its behavior for a specific task or customer. A deployment serving many LoRA variants for the same base model must route each request to a replica that already has the required LoRA loaded in GPU memory. Routing without this awareness forces constant LoRA swapping, adding latency and reducing throughput on each affected replica.

resources.title: Unsupervised LoRA Routing
Intelligent LoRA Routing
What is Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA)

subtopics.name: Capacity Management
subtopics.description: Multi-cloud inference pools GPU capacity from multiple cloud providers and regions into a single schedulable resource, treating distinct compute pools as fungible. This requires a global control plane for deployment and scaling decisions alongside per-cluster workload planes that serve traffic and report utilization. True multi-cloud unlocks greater total capacity, improved reliability through redundancy, lower latency via geographic proximity, and data sovereignty compliance.

resources.title: How we built Multi-cloud Capacity Management (MCM)
Multi-cloud capacity management

subtopics.name: Request Queueing
subtopics.description: A request queue holds incoming traffic when all active replicas are at capacity while autoscaling brings new replicas online. A first-in, first-out queue is the standard implementation; priority queues can give paid users better position. Queues must be visible to newly started replicas so that requests are not held waiting for existing replicas when new capacity becomes available.

resources.title: Efficient Request Queueing – Optimizing LLM Performance
LLM Request Queuing
Why Do AI Requests Queue? | Inside vLLM

subtopics.name: Geo-Aware Load Balancing
subtopics.description: A global load balancer routes requests to the GPU cluster geographically closest to the requesting user. Network latency accumulates at roughly 5 milliseconds per time zone traversed, so routing a request from Singapore to San Francisco adds 50 to 100 milliseconds of unnecessary overhead. Geo-aware routing ensures that spare capacity in a distant region is used only when nearby capacity is exhausted.

resources.title: How Geographic Load Balancing Improves Performance
Geo-aware load balancing

subtopics.name: Scale to Zero
subtopics.description: Scale to zero allows the system to run zero replicas during periods of no traffic and spin up on demand. It requires fast cold starts and robust queuing to hold incoming requests while a replica starts. Scale to zero is well-suited for development environments and periodically accessed workloads, but not for latency-sensitive production applications with unpredictable light traffic.

resources.title: Should LLM Serving Scale to Zero for Cost

topics.name: Testing & Deployment
topics.description: Deploying inference services safely requires tools for rolling out changes without downtime, estimating costs before committing to a configuration, and maintaining visibility into system health once live. This group covers the deployment, cost, observability, and compliance concerns that apply once a service is ready for production traffic.

resources.title: Testing and Deployment AI Models

subtopics.name: Security and Compliance
subtopics.description: Inference infrastructure must protect user inputs, model outputs, and model weights. Standard practices include data encryption, container security, network isolation, and access controls validated by third-party penetration testing. Regulated industries require compliance with frameworks like SOC 2 and HIPAA, which also apply to underlying cloud providers. Multi-cloud deployments support data residency requirements by routing each country's data to clusters in that country.

resources.title: Inference security: How to protect APIs in production AI systems
How to achieve compliance and security in AI inference
Are your AI Inference and GenAI Environments Secure? These Five Essentials Will Help

subtopics.name: Indep. Component Scaling
subtopics.description: Multi-model pipelines, like a voice agent that runs VAD, ASR, an LLM, and TTS in sequence, have components with different hardware requirements and traffic patterns. Each component should autoscale independently based on its own load. Running all components within the same Kubernetes cluster minimizes inter-component network latency, which can otherwise consume a significant fraction of a tight latency budget.

resources.title: Autoscaling Workloads
Autoscaling endpoints for LLM inference
Intro to Kubernetes Autoscaling and Best Practices for Implementations

subtopics.name: Zero-Downtime Deplo.
subtopics.description: Canary deployments update inference services without interrupting live traffic by routing a small percentage of requests to the new deployment, monitoring for issues, and gradually shifting traffic over. Blue-green deployments, which cut all traffic at once to a parallel environment, are impractical for large inference workloads because they require doubling GPU capacity during the transition. With autoscaling, canary deployments are low cost since the old service scales down as the new one takes traffic.

Zero Downtime Deployments in Kubernetes Explained

subtopics.name: Cost Estimation
subtopics.description: Dedicated inference cost depends on batch sizing, traffic patterns, and sequence lengths rather than simply on token count. Comparing dedicated versus API costs requires converting per-token API pricing into total cost over a representative time window and comparing it to GPU-hour costs at the same traffic volume. Total cost of ownership also includes engineering time for building and maintaining the inference system.

resources.title: The Hidden Economics of LLM Inference
LLM Inference Benchmarking: How Much Does Your LLM Inference Cost?
LLM inference cost: what drives it and how to lower it
LLM Cost Calculation Guide for Enterprise AI Teams in 2026

subtopics.name: Observability
subtopics.description: Inference observability tracks total request volume, input and output sequence lengths, response codes, latency percentiles (P50, P90, P99 of TTFT, TPS, and end-to-end latency), replica count, GPU utilization, and queue depth. These metrics are interdependent; a latency spike could come from long input sequences, high concurrency, or a hardware issue. Observability must integrate with existing tooling like Grafana, Datadog, and PagerDuty to put inference metrics in context.

nodes.name: Introduction
nodes.description: Inference engineering is the practice of making generative AI models faster, less expensive, and more reliable to serve in production. It spans the full stack from CUDA kernels and GPU architecture to Kubernetes autoscaling and multi-cloud capacity management. The field emerged alongside the explosion of open models and the shift from pay-per-token APIs to dedicated deployments, where engineers own latency, throughput, cost, and uptime directly.

resources.title: Inference Engineering

AI Inference: The Secret to AI's Superpowers

nodes.name: Open vs Closed Models
nodes.description: Closed models are accessed exclusively through a vendor API; the weights are never released. Open models publish their weights for download and self-hosting. For inference engineers, this distinction determines the entire problem space: closed models require no infrastructure but offer no control over latency, cost, or configuration, while open models require building and operating a full inference stack but give complete control over every layer of it.

resources.title: AI Engineering: Building Applications with Foundation Models

nodes.name: Inference vs. Training
nodes.description: Training is the process of learning model weights from data. Inference is serving those weights in production to generate outputs. Training runs are compute-intensive batch jobs; inference is a continuous, latency-sensitive service. Where training success is measured in loss curves, inference success is measured in time to first token, tokens per second, and uptime.

resources.title: Language Models Are Few-Shot Learners
Inference vs Training

Why Inference is hard..

nodes.name: Time to First Token
nodes.description: TTFT measures how long it takes for a user to receive the first output token after submitting a request. It is determined primarily by the prefill phase and by queue time. For streaming applications like chatbots, TTFT is the most visible latency signal and directly affects perceived responsiveness.

resources.title: What is time to first token (TTFT)?
What Is Time to First Token?
Most devs don't understand how LLM tokens work

nodes.name: Tokens Per Second
nodes.description: TPS measures how many tokens are delivered to the user per second after the first token. It is determined by the decode phase and reflects memory bandwidth efficiency. Per-user TPS (also called perceived TPS) is a latency metric; total TPS across the inference service is a throughput metric.

resources.title: What Are Tokens per Second?
Tokens Per Second
LLM Speed Tiers Explained: What TPS (Token Per Second) Actually Feels Like

nodes.name: Inter-Token Latency
nodes.description: ITL is the time between successive generated tokens during decode. An ITL of 10 milliseconds corresponds to 100 tokens per second. It is the per-step measure underlying TPS and is directly tied to how quickly the GPU can complete a single decode forward pass.

resources.title: Inter-Token Latency - NVIDIA
Inter-Token Latency

nodes.name: Latency vs. Throughput
nodes.description: Lower latency means faster responses per user; higher throughput means more total requests served per unit time. These goals are often in tension. Increasing batch size improves throughput but worsens per-user latency. Choosing the right balance is one of the primary decisions in configuring an inference service.

resources.title: The LLM Inference Trilemma: Throughput, Latency, Cost

Latency vs Throughput in 60 Seconds

nodes.name: Latency Percentiles
nodes.description: Mean latency hides outliers. LLM response times follow a right-skewed distribution, so engineers measure P50, P90, P95, and P99. A P99 of several seconds means one in a hundred users has a poor experience even if the median is fast. Reducing P90/P99 latency is as important as reducing average latency.

resources.title: Percentiles vs averages: why your latency dashboard lies
Latency percentiles for load testing analysis
Mastering Latency Metrics: P90, P95, P99 | System Design

nodes.name: End-to-End Metrics
nodes.description: End-to-end latency includes inference time, network round-trip, queue time, and client-side overhead. Inference-only metrics tell you how well the model server performs; end-to-end metrics tell you what users actually experience. When inference time is fast but end-to-end time is slow, the bottleneck is in infrastructure or client code, not the GPU.

resources.title: 10 LLM Inference Metrics Every AI Engineer Must Know

nodes.name: Real-Time Factor
nodes.description: RTF measures how quickly an ASR system can process audio relative to its duration. A system that transcribes one hour of audio in six seconds has an RTF of 600x. It is the standard throughput metric for long-file transcription workloads and improves roughly linearly with the number of GPUs used for parallel chunk processing.

nodes.name: Shared vs. Dedicated Inf.
nodes.description: Shared inference means sending requests to a public API and paying per token. Dedicated inference means renting GPUs and running your own model server, paying per GPU-hour. Shared inference is simpler and has no cold start, but dedicated inference offers control over latency, cost at scale, model customization, and uptime. Most products start shared and move to dedicated as traffic grows.

nodes.name: The Inference Stack
nodes.description: A complete inference system has three layers: runtime, infrastructure, and tooling. The runtime layer optimizes a single model on a single instance using techniques like batching, caching, quantization, and speculation. The infrastructure layer scales across clusters, regions, and cloud providers while maintaining uptime. The tooling layer provides the right level of abstraction for engineers to control the system productively. All three must work together for mission-critical inference at scale.

nodes.name: Prefill & Decode Phases
nodes.description: LLM inference has two distinct phases. Prefill processes the entire input sequence in parallel to build the KV cache and is compute-bound. Decode generates output tokens one at a time by reading model weights from memory and is memory-bound. Each phase has different bottlenecks and responds to different optimization techniques.

nodes.name: Online vs. Offline Inf.
nodes.description: Online inference serves real-time user-facing requests where latency matters. Offline inference processes large batches of data asynchronously where throughput and cost matter more than per-request speed. The same model, like Whisper for transcription, may need separate deployments for each use case because the optimal configurations differ significantly.

resources.title: Production ML systems: Static versus dynamic inference

nodes.name: Asynchronous Inference
nodes.description: Asynchronous inference is a fire-and-forget request model where the client submits a job, receives an immediate acknowledgment, and retrieves the result later via a webhook. It is suited for throughput-sensitive, latency-insensitive workloads like bulk document embedding or corpus transcription. Async jobs have much longer time limits than synchronous requests and require robust server-side queuing.

resources.title: Using asynchronous inference in production
Asynchronous Inference: Methods & Applications

nodes.name: AI-Native Applications
nodes.description: AI-native applications are products where generative models power the core user experience, from code editors and voice agents to customer support and media generation. Each category has different inference requirements. Agents generate many inference calls per user action; chat applications prioritize TTFT; voice applications need low end-to-end latency for natural conversation.

nodes.name: Consumer vs. B2B
nodes.description: Consumer applications are cost-sensitive and have unpredictable traffic spikes, requiring flexible autoscaling and low marginal cost. Business-to-business applications prioritize uptime and consistent low latency, as they often sit in the critical path of revenue-generating workflows. Compliance requirements, including data residency and regulatory certifications, are more common in enterprise deployments.

resources.title: Consumer vs. B2B

nodes.name: Reasoning Models
nodes.description: Reasoning models generate an intermediate thinking sequence before producing their final output, adding a third token sequence alongside the input and output. This reasoning trace increases total token count significantly and changes inference economics: TTFT is higher, total latency is longer, and output token costs dominate. Inference engineers must account for the variable and sometimes very long reasoning sequences when sizing infrastructure and setting latency budgets.

nodes.name: Model Selection
nodes.description: The most important decision in model performance optimization is which model to use. Smaller models with fewer parameters are faster and cheaper to serve than larger ones. The goal is to find the smallest model that meets quality requirements for the task. Model architecture also determines which inference engines and optimization techniques are available, so popular architectures with broad tooling support are preferable.

nodes.name: Model Evaluation
nodes.description: Model evaluation, or evals, is the practice of systematically measuring model quality for a specific task or domain. Standard intelligence benchmarks like MMLU measure general capabilities but can be gamed; product-specific evals that test real use cases provide more reliable signal. High-confidence evals are a prerequisite before investing in inference optimization, ensuring the model is actually useful before making it fast.

resources.title: LLM Evaluation: A Beginner's Guide

nodes.name: Fine-Tuning
nodes.description: Fine-tuning takes a pretrained foundation model and adapts it to a specific domain by training on additional labeled data. A small fine-tuned model can match a much larger general model on constrained tasks like text-to-SQL. Smaller models are faster and cheaper to serve, so fine-tuning is one of the highest-leverage tools for hitting latency and cost targets.

nodes.name: Distillation
nodes.description: Distillation trains a smaller student model to emulate a larger teacher model by exposing it to the teacher's probability distributions, not just its final outputs. Unlike fine-tuning on synthetic data, distillation transfers the teacher's reasoning behavior. The resulting student model is smaller and faster while retaining much of the teacher's quality on the same tasks.

nodes.name: Compute
nodes.description: A GPU's compute capability is determined by its Streaming Multiprocessors (SMs), each containing CUDA Cores for general arithmetic and Tensor Cores for matrix multiply-accumulate operations. Tensor Cores are the primary resource for inference, executing the matmuls that make up the majority of forward pass computation. GPU compute is measured in peak Tensor Core FLOPS at a given precision, and roughly doubles with each new NVIDIA architecture generation.

nodes.name: Neural Networks
nodes.description: A neural network is a layered structure of nodes where each node applies a learned weight matrix and bias to its input. Multiple layers connected in sequence form the foundation for all generative AI models. Inference engineers need a working model of how neural networks compute outputs to understand where performance bottlenecks arise.

nodes.name: Encoder-Decoder Arch.
nodes.description: Neural networks can be organized as encoder-only, decoder-only, or encoder-decoder models. Modern LLMs are decoder-only. Encoder-only models like BERT are used for text embeddings and classification. Encoder-decoder models like Whisper use an encoder to process input into an internal representation and a decoder to generate output tokens autoregressively. Each architecture has different inference characteristics and tooling requirements.

nodes.name: Large Language Models
nodes.description: An LLM is a decoder-only transformer with three main components: an embedding layer that converts input tokens to vectors, a stack of transformer blocks that process those vectors, and an output language modeling head that converts the final hidden states into a probability distribution over the vocabulary. The configuration file for an open model specifies all architectural details including layer count, hidden dimensions, and attention heads.

nodes.name: Transformer Blocks
nodes.description: Transformer blocks are the repeated hidden layers of an LLM. Each block contains an attention sublayer, a feed-forward neural network sublayer, and normalization layers. The feed-forward network holds the majority of model parameters, while attention is the most computationally complex operation per token.

resources.title: Attention Is All You Need

nodes.name: Attention Mechanism
nodes.description: Attention is the mechanism transformers use to relate each token to all previous tokens via query, key, and value projections. During decode, each new token attends to every prior token, and the KV cache stores precomputed keys and values to avoid recomputation. Attention is the most expensive and most heavily optimized operation in LLM inference.

nodes.name: KV Cache
nodes.description: The KV cache stores the key and value tensors computed during attention for each previously processed token. Without it, attention would require recomputing every prior token on each decode step, making inference prohibitively slow. The KV cache lives in GPU memory and its size grows with sequence length and batch size, making it a major target for memory management techniques.

nodes.name: Mixture of Experts (MoE)
nodes.description: Mixture of Experts models replace dense linear layers with a set of smaller expert matrices, activating only a subset of experts per token via a learned router. A model like Qwen3-235B activates only 22 billion of its 235 billion parameters per forward pass, making single-user inference efficient. In batched production serving, different tokens activate different experts, so nearly all parameters are active across the batch.

nodes.name: Image & Video Models
nodes.description: Image and video models are specialized artificial intelligence architectures designed to process, interpret, and generate visual data. These models utilize techniques like convolutional neural networks (CNNs), transformers, and diffusion processes to analyze pixel patterns for tasks such as object detection, image classification, and video frame synthesis.

nodes.name: Diffusion Models
nodes.description: Diffusion models generate images by starting from random noise and iteratively denoising it over 30 to 50 steps, guided by a text prompt. Each step runs the denoiser twice, once with conditioning and once without, to apply classifier-free guidance. The entire process operates in a low-dimensional latent space rather than full pixel space to make attention computationally feasible.

nodes.name: Image Generation Arch.
nodes.description: Image generation models are pipelines of multiple components: a text encoder that converts the prompt into conditioning, a denoising model that iteratively refines a latent representation from noise into an image, and a variational autoencoder that converts the final latent to pixels. The denoising model is the largest and most compute-intensive component and runs up to 100 forward passes per image generation.

nodes.name: Few-Step Image Generation
nodes.description: Few-step image generation models produce usable images in eight or fewer denoising steps by training the model to collapse the standard 30 to 50 step process into a fraction of the iterations. Techniques include latent consistency distillation and adversarial training, both of which teach the model to reach high-quality outputs in fewer passes. They are a strong fit for latency-sensitive use cases like real-time filters, but produce noticeably lower quality than full-step models and are a model selection decision rather than an inference optimization technique.

nodes.name: Video Generation Models
nodes.description: Video generation models extend image generation to three-dimensional latent space, representing width, height, and time simultaneously. They run the same number of denoising steps as image models but process far more data per step. Attention over the full video latent space dominates compute time, making video generation the most resource-intensive common inference workload.

nodes.name: Bottleneck Analysis
nodes.description: Bottleneck analysis identifies whether a given inference workload is limited by compute or by memory bandwidth, which determines which optimizations will actually improve performance. The core tool is the ops:byte ratio: comparing a GPU's peak FLOPS against its peak memory bandwidth reveals the hardware's balance point, and comparing a model operation's arithmetic intensity against that balance point reveals whether it is compute-bound or memory-bound. LLM prefill and image generation are compute-bound; LLM decode is memory-bound.

nodes.name: Ops:Byte Ratio
nodes.description: The ops:byte ratio is a property of GPU hardware that expresses the balance between compute throughput and memory bandwidth. It is calculated by dividing peak FLOPS by peak memory bandwidth, and sets the threshold that separates compute-bound from memory-bound workloads on that device. Different GPU generations have very different ops:byte ratios, which is why an optimization that works well on one generation may have no effect on another.

resources.title: A guide to LLM inference and performance
Understanding Performance

nodes.name: Arithmetic Intensity
nodes.description: Arithmetic intensity is a property of an algorithm: the number of floating-point operations performed per byte of memory read or written. A large matrix multiplication has high arithmetic intensity because the same weights participate in many operations per load; a decode forward pass has low arithmetic intensity because each weight is loaded from VRAM and used once per token. Comparing a workload's arithmetic intensity against the GPU's ops:byte ratio is the fastest way to diagnose whether adding compute or adding bandwidth would help.

resources.title: A guide to LLM inference and performance

nodes.name: Roofline Model
nodes.description: The roofline model is a visual framework for reasoning about hardware performance limits. It plots arithmetic intensity on the x-axis against achievable performance on the y-axis, with two ceilings: a diagonal memory bandwidth ceiling for low-intensity workloads and a horizontal compute ceiling for high-intensity ones. A workload's position relative to these ceilings shows not just whether it is compute-bound or memory-bound, but how far it sits from the hardware's theoretical maximum — which tells you how much headroom remains before an optimization hits a hard limit.

nodes.name: LLM Bottlenecks
nodes.description: LLM prefill is compute-bound because it processes the entire input sequence as one large matrix multiplication, performing many operations per byte loaded. LLM decode is memory-bound because it generates tokens one at a time via vector-matrix multiplications that require loading all model weights from memory for each token while performing relatively few arithmetic operations.

nodes.name: Attention Optimization
nodes.description: Attention optimization refers to techniques designed to improve the computational efficiency and memory usage of the attention mechanism within transformer models. Because standard attention scales quadratically with input sequence length, these optimizations aim to reduce computation and memory overhead. By streamlining how tokens interact with one another, these methods allow models to process longer inputs faster and run on hardware with less available memory.

nodes.name: Image & Video Bottlenecks
nodes.description: Image and video generation models are compute-bound because each denoising step applies attention over the entire latent space in parallel, similar to LLM prefill. The models are also relatively small, so memory bandwidth is not the limiting factor. Optimizations focus on FLOPS efficiency rather than memory traffic reduction.

nodes.name: FlashAttention
nodes.description: FlashAttention is a series of hand-optimized CUDA kernels that compute attention with fewer reads and writes to GPU memory by fusing the attention algorithm into a single kernel. Standard attention stores intermediate matrices to memory between steps; FlashAttention eliminates those round-trips. FlashAttention 3 targets Hopper GPUs and FlashAttention 4 targets Blackwell GPUs.

nodes.name: PagedAttention
nodes.description: PagedAttention stores the KV cache in fixed-size pages rather than a single contiguous memory block, allowing it to be distributed across GPU memory without fragmentation. It uses a lookup table to access pages on demand, reducing memory waste from over-allocation and enabling more requests to share GPU memory. It is the memory management technique that made vLLM's high throughput possible.

nodes.name: Attention Variants
nodes.description: Newer attention algorithms reduce the quadratic time complexity of standard attention. Sliding window attention limits each token to attending to the nearest w tokens, turning O(N²) into O(Nw). Linear attention approximates the softmax with a linear-time kernel. Compressed attention periodically compresses earlier context. These variants trade off some quality for better scaling on long sequences.

nodes.description: GPU architecture determines the hard limits of what inference can achieve on a given device. This group covers compute, memory, interconnects, and sizing — the four dimensions an inference engineer needs to understand to make informed decisions about hardware selection, parallelism strategy, and optimization priorities.

nodes.name: Memory
nodes.description: GPU memory determines what fits on a single device and how fast data can move through the compute units. VRAM capacity sets the upper limit on model size and KV cache; VRAM bandwidth determines how quickly the decode phase can load weights per token. Modern datacenter GPUs use high-bandwidth memory (HBM) in generations HBM3, HBM3e, and HBM4, stacked directly on the GPU die to maximize bandwidth.

nodes.description: The Hopper architecture, released in 2022 with the H100 and later the H200, introduced FP8 Tensor Cores offering twice the compute throughput of FP16 and asynchronous data transfer features used by FlashAttention 3. H100 and H200 GPUs remain among the most widely deployed inference accelerators due to their maturity, broad software support, and relative availability compared to newer generations.

nodes.name: Blackwell
nodes.description: The Blackwell architecture, released in late 2024 with the B200 and B300, added FP4 Tensor Cores and new microscaling number formats including MXFP8, MXFP4, and NVFP4. B200 GPUs offer approximately 5 petaFLOPS of FP8 compute and up to 8 TB/s of memory bandwidth. They are the current gold standard for demanding inference workloads including large LLMs and video generation.

nodes.name: Instances & Interconnects
nodes.description: Within a node, NVLink connects GPUs one-to-one at up to 1800 GB/s on Blackwell, and NVSwitch creates an all-to-all fabric across all eight GPUs. Between nodes, InfiniBand provides inter-node connectivity at substantially lower bandwidth than NVLink. Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) partitions a single GPU into up to seven isolated slices, each with dedicated compute and memory, allowing small models to run on fractions of a high-end GPU without resource contention.

nodes.name: Sizing & Procurement
nodes.description: Estimating GPU requirements starts with VRAM: roughly 1 GB per billion parameters at FP8 for weights, plus at least 50 percent headroom for the KV cache. This total is rounded up to the nearest available instance size. Cloud GPUs are available from hyperscalers like AWS and GCP, neoclouds like CoreWeave and Nebius, and spot markets; large deployments combine reserved instances for baseline load with on-demand and spot capacity for bursts.

nodes.description: NVIDIA's ARM-based Grace and Vera CPUs connect to their paired GPUs via NVLink Chip-to-Chip at up to 900 GB/s, far higher than standard PCIe connections. This high-bandwidth CPU-GPU link makes offloading KV caches and LoRA weights to CPU memory practical, since data can be retrieved quickly enough to remain on the critical path. nodes.name: Desktop Inference
nodes.description: Desktop inference runs on consumer hardware, primarily Apple M-series unified memory systems and high-end NVIDIA consumer GPUs. Apple hardware offers very large unified memory capacity at moderate bandwidth, enabling larger models than discrete consumer GPUs; NVIDIA consumer GPUs offer higher bandwidth with smaller capacity. Hardware limitations restrict practical model sizes to one to two billion parameters on current phones. Small fine-tuned models for tasks like transcription, translation, and on-device classification are the strongest fit for mobile edge inference.

nodes.name: CUDA
nodes.description: CUDA is NVIDIA's proprietary platform for programming GPUs, consisting of a kernel language (C++), a driver for hardware management, and a runtime API for launching kernels. Every inference engine, framework, and library in the NVIDIA ecosystem depends on CUDA, including cuBLAS — NVIDIA's optimized implementation of standard linear algebra routines and the default backend for matrix multiplications in most inference pipelines. Understanding CUDA is the foundation for diagnosing performance problems that tools and engines cannot solve automatically.

nodes.name: Kernel Selection & Fusion
nodes.description: A CUDA kernel is a function that runs in parallel across thousands of GPU threads simultaneously. Kernel selection is choosing the best existing kernel for a specific operation; kernel fusion combines sequential kernels into one to eliminate unnecessary reads and writes to VRAM between operations. Libraries like cuBLAS, CUTLASS, CuTe, and FlashInfer provide pre-built kernels for common inference operations, and most inference engines perform kernel selection automatically.

nodes.name: Writing Custom Kernels
nodes.description: Custom kernels are written when existing libraries do not fully utilize a GPU's capabilities for a specific operation or architecture. Most production kernels are written in C++ using CUTLASS and CuTe for GEMM-style operations and FlashInfer for attention variants; Triton offers a Python-based alternative with a lower barrier to entry. Writing an effective kernel requires understanding the target GPU's memory hierarchy, SM occupancy, and Tensor Core instruction set — skills that sit at the intersection of software and hardware.

nodes.name: PyTorch
nodes.description: PyTorch is the standard Python framework for building and running neural networks. It abstracts CUDA into a tensor operation API and provides automatic differentiation for training. For inference, PyTorch supports torch.compile for automatic kernel optimization and serves as the foundation that all major inference engines build on top of.

nodes.description: Safetensors is the standard format for storing and distributing open model weights. It uses memory mapping for fast, zero-copy loading and prevents execution of arbitrary code during deserialization, making it safer than earlier pickle-based formats. All major inference engines load safetensors natively, and most open models on Hugging Face publish weights in this format.

nodes.name: TensorRT
nodes.description: TensorRT is NVIDIA's high-performance inference runtime that compiles PyTorch or ONNX models into optimized engines using fused kernels, quantization, and hardware-specific tuning. It is the standard choice for image and video generation models and for any workload where maximum throughput on NVIDIA hardware is the primary goal. Compiled engines are cached to disk, eliminating recompilation overhead on subsequent cold starts.

SGLang Diffusion extends it to image and video generation models with pipeline abstractions and diffusion-specific parallelism.

They implement continuous batching, memory management, parallelism, and optimization techniques so engineers do not have to implement these from scratch. Its primary advantage is ease of adoption and the fastest day-zero support for newly released open models. It also supports multimodal inference via vLLM Omni.

It achieves the highest performance among the three major engines, with excellent support for Hopper and Blackwell architectures and NVIDIA-specific formats like NVFP4. In inference benchmarking it is used to simulate realistic user traffic patterns — including request arrival rates, concurrency ramps, and burst scenarios — that synthetic tools do not capture. nodes.name: Quantization
nodes.description: Quantization converts model weights and other values from their native precision to a lower-precision format. Cutting precision in half doubles memory bandwidth for decode and enables twice the FLOPS for prefill on compatible Tensor Cores. The tradeoff is potential quality loss from reduced numerical precision, which can compound across the many calculations in a forward pass.

This produces better quality at low precision than post-training quantization but requires retraining the model from scratch or from a checkpoint. Some labs release models trained this way, such as GPT-OSS in MXFP4.

It is the standard approach for most deployments since it requires no retraining and can be applied to any existing model. The leading tool is NVIDIA ModelOpt, which exports quantized models in formats compatible with all major inference engines.

nodes.name: Speculative Decoding
nodes.description: Speculative decoding takes advantage of spare compute during memory-bound decode by generating multiple draft tokens and validating them in a single forward pass. If the target model accepts N draft tokens, the forward pass produces N+1 tokens instead of one. The performance gain depends on draft token cost, draft sequence length, and acceptance rate, which decreases at higher temperatures and larger batch sizes.

nodes.name: N-gram
nodes.description: N-gram speculation builds a dictionary during prefill that maps token prefixes to observed n-gram continuations from the input. During decode, generated tokens are looked up in this dictionary and matching suffixes become draft tokens with no separate model required. It is most effective for code completion, where output frequently mirrors input syntax, and can produce very long draft sequences with high acceptance rates in that domain.

nodes.name: Draft-Target Decoding
nodes.description: Draft-target speculation uses a small draft model, typically at least ten times smaller than the target, to generate draft tokens for the target model to verify. The draft model should share the same tokenizer and general behavior as the target, often being a smaller member of the same model family. It is the simplest speculation method to set up but introduces the most overhead due to running a separate model.

nodes.name: EAGLE
nodes.description: EAGLE is a purpose-built speculation method where a small draft model is trained to accept hidden states from the target model as input. By seeing the target's internal representations, EAGLE achieves higher acceptance rates and longer draft sequences (up to eight tokens) than using a general-purpose small model. It integrates into the same forward pass as the target model, eliminating the orchestration overhead of separate draft and target model runs.

nodes.name: Caching
nodes.description: Caching reuses previously computed KV values to avoid redundant prefill computation across requests that share common context. It is one of the most impactful techniques for reducing TTFT in workloads with long system prompts or multi-turn conversations. This group covers the approaches, storage tiers, routing implications, and long-context strategies that make caching effective at scale.

nodes.name: Caching Approaches
nodes.description: KV cache reuse is the primary caching strategy in LLM inference, covering both prefix caching (reusing cached KV values across requests that share a common prefix) and KV cache offloading (moving less-used cache blocks to slower storage tiers to free GPU VRAM). A related concern is cache-aware routing, which directs requests to replicas most likely to already hold the relevant cached prefix.
